Witness statement of [MOTHER OF BABY Q] (read)

May it please your Lordship, members of the jury, we are, as you know, about to move on to the next, and indeed final, count on the indictment. If I could invite you to take your jury bundle number 1 and go behind divider 1. You'll find the indictment, the final page of which, page 8, has the details of count 22: an allegation of attempted murder, dated the 25th day of June 2016 in relation to the baby [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: May I begin, my Lord, by reading the statement of [Baby Q]'s mother, a statement made in the name of [Mother of Baby Q], now known as [Mother of Baby Q], a statement dated 8 November 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am the mother of [Baby Q], born at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 22 June 2016 at 04.09 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I initially discovered that I was pregnant in November 2015 when I was 4 weeks' gestation. I would describe that the pregnancy was difficult and at 8 weeks' gestation I was in a great deal of pain and it was thought that I may have an ectopic pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I first went to the Countess of Chester Hospital, the staff told me that everything was okay without giving me a scan. I pushed for a scan and they told me that I would have one the following week so I was sent home.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I had a scan at 9 weeks and 2 days, everything appeared okay inside the womb. However, when the outside of the womb was scanned, a problem was found, and senior staff were sent for.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was told that I had a heterotopic pregnancy. This means that one twin was inside the womb and one twin was growing outside the womb. Due to the seriousness of the condition I was sent for surgery and [Baby Q]'s twin was removed. The baby had been growing inside the fallopian tube, so this was also removed in order to save myself and [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From 9 weeks' gestation to 26 weeks' gestation I was unable to work, but everything was fine. When I reached 26 weeks I was admitted to the Countess of Chester Hospital suffering from heavy bleeding and was then admitted and not allowed to leave the hospital until [Baby Q] was delivered at 31 weeks due to a placental abruption.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It had been intended that [Baby Q] be delivered at 34 weeks. However, the placental abruption changed this. When I went down to surgery, which was for a seventh time, I was told at this point it was only a small bleed. However, I then had a heavy bleed, which turned into an emergency situation, where I had wires and drips all over me in my arms and neck.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I had asked for [Father of Baby Q] [and you'll hear that is [Baby Q]'s father] to attend due to the situation. I was put under general anaesthetic in order to have the procedure. I recall that when I woke up from anaesthetic, I had to wait for 12 hours before I could go and see [Baby Q]. I was reliant on other people to help me.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was told that [Baby Q] was on a ventilator to help his breathing. During the pregnancy, I was given steroids in order to mature his lungs due to his prematurity. After his birth, [Baby Q] was placed under a jaundice lamp in room 1 on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Room 1 is for the most ill babies and is the highest dependency room in the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] had wires into his belly button, a feeding tube, an oxygen mask/tube directly into his airway, and a cannula in his hand. I remember that I was taken to the neonatal unit of the hospital at around 4 pm that day. Once there, I didn't get to hold him, but was able to put my hands through the side of the incubator. When I talked to him, he opened his eyes for the first time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On day 3 after his birth, [Baby Q] was taken off the oxygen and moved to room 2. He was breathing on his own with no aid from a ventilator. He still had a feeding tube and a jaundice light.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At the end of that day we were told that he would have to go back on to oxygen and back into room 1. I was really upset at this point and far too upset to go down to see him. Therefore [Father of Baby Q] went down to the unit. We were not told of any issue with [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The staff told [Father of Baby Q] that their main priority was to treat [Baby Q] and at no point did they say that they were saving [Baby Q]'s life or that he had had a collapse. I think that they played everything down to protect the parents and prevent panic.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When [Baby Q] was about 1 week of age, he was sent to Alder Hey Hospital to be seen by the surgeons as it was possible that part of his bowel might have needed to be removed. Luckily, this did not happen and [Baby Q] was treated by antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "He was not allowed milk or feeds, had cannulas in his feet and both hands, so that he was getting enough fluids into his body. [Baby Q] did not have any milk for over a week and we had to wait until his stomach contents were clear in colour until he could feed again."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Turning to page 4, my Lord, his mother now gives some narrative about his young life after hospital:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In terms of [Baby Q]'s health, he has been in and out of hospital many times, at least three times a year as an inpatient with various infections as he has a weakened immune system.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In August 2018 [Baby Q] was diagnosed with a right sided hemiplegic cerebral palsy and may have autism and is under a specialist."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That concludes the relevant parts of [Baby Q]'s mother's statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of [FATHER OF BABY Q] (read)
Turning to a statement made by his father, [Father of Baby Q], dated 12 December 2019:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am the father of [Baby Q], born at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 22 June 2016 at 04.09 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My wife [Mother of Baby Q] had a very difficult pregnancy with [Baby Q]. We were not aware until she was 9 weeks pregnant that there was a second baby, which had formed in the fallopian tube, which is classed as an ectopic pregnancy. [Mother of Baby Q] had been suffering from pain and this was the reason for the hospital visit. She had a keyhole operation to remove the foetus from her right fallopian tube. From this point onwards, [Mother of Baby Q] was in and out of hospital every 6 weeks or so.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When she reached 26 weeks, [Mother of Baby Q] was taken into the Countess of Chester Hospital due to very heavy bleeding. At first, I think she was in the labour ward whilst they made sure that [Baby Q] was okay and then, having had drugs to stop her going into labour, she was put on another ward in the women's and children's department of the hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In the period of 26 weeks to 31 weeks, when [Baby Q] was born, there were a number of occasions when [Mother of Baby Q] would have heavy bleeding and would be rushed downstairs to the labour ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 22 June 2016, in the middle of the night, I got a phone call to say that [Baby Q] was going to be born. I arrived to [Mother
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: of Baby Q] bleeding very heavily. I didn't get much time with [Mother of Baby Q] as she was being rushed to theatre. I was not allowed into the theatre because it was not a normal caesarean section operation. I had to wait outside on the corridor outside the theatre. After possibly an hour, or maybe more, I saw a baby being wheeled out of the theatre in an incubator. I asked the staff whether it was my baby and they said yes. He was tiny at 4 pounds and 4 ounces.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I asked how [Mother of Baby Q] was. She was still under anaesthetic and then in recovery. During this time, I went to the neonatal unit to see [Baby Q] and to get some photographs before coming back to see [Mother of Baby Q], who had come round and was asking about him. It was some time before [Mother of Baby Q] was able to go in and see him, so I kept going in to see him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It was some hours before [Mother of Baby Q] was able to see [Baby Q] as she was not able to get up and get into a wheelchair. Once she was able to go in, numerous staff would take her to the neonatal unit to visit [Baby Q], which was a lift journey and short corridor away. He was on that unit for a total of 5 weeks.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] started off in room 1 because he was so premature and needed intensive care. [Baby Q] was progressing well and was coming off the ventilator but was still tube-fed in room 1.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Approximately 1 to 2 weeks after [Baby Q] was born, I went down to the neonatal unit to see him. I got through the main door to the unit but was stopped from gaining access to room 1.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "One of the staff had stopped me and I asked them what was going on. I was told that there was nothing to worry about, that he had a chest infection and that they wanted to make sure that he was suitable for a visit. When anything happens on the unit, it is all screened off and shut down.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I went back to see [Mother of Baby Q] and told her what had happened. She got into a wheelchair and we went straight down to the neonatal unit to see what was happening.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When we got down to the unit, we were told that they would inform us when we were able to see [Baby Q] and I think they told us that they were running some tests. We went back upstairs to the ward and waited.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We were informed a short time later that [Baby Q] was okay for a visit, so we went back downstairs. He was back on the breathing apparatus, which he had previously come off. We asked the doctor what had happened and he said there had been a blip
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: with his breathing and he had become tired and to help him have a rest, they had to put him back on the ventilator. We were happy that they were paying attention to [Baby Q] and that they were helping him to get rest when he was tired. We didn't think any more of it. It would have been in the afternoon that this had happened.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After this, we got back to hoping that [Baby Q] would progress again. After approximately 2 to 3 weeks, [Baby Q] was moved into room 2. When we visited him one day we were told that he had a serious bowel infection. We were allowed to see him straightaway and nothing on the unit was cordoned off like the first incident, even though he needed emergency surgery and was awaiting a specialist ambulance to go to Alder Hey Hospital where the specialists were.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "By the time he had got to Alder Hey Hospital, he had recovered and the surgeon said that he was okay. He was then sent back the same day to the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Once back, he was in room 1 again, but he recovered really well and there were no issues. The following day, he was moved to room 2 and then recovered to be released from hospital after 5 weeks."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At page 5 of [Father of Baby Q]'s statement, my Lord, he summarises:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby Q] has disabilities which include mild hemiplegic cerebral palsy on his right side."

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS SUSAN DILLON (read)

My Lord, two statements to read, please, by way of beginning this afternoon. The first one is at page 11 of my Lord's bundle, it's a statement from Susan Dillon. It's dated 12 April 2018 and she says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am a registered midwife, having qualified in 2007. Between April 2011 and December 2016 I worked as a midwife at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 02.05 hours on Wednesday, 22 June 2016 I was on duty in the labour ward when the care of [Mother of Baby Q] was handed over to me from the postnatal ward. [Mother of Baby Q] had placenta previa and was bleeding. We estimated that she had already lost 200ml of blood. There was concern that the placenta had started to detach from the uterine wall. [Mother of Baby Q]'s observations (blood pressure, pulse and temperature) were all in normal limits, but at this time she was complaining of a tender abdomen.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 02.45 I contacted [Mother of Baby Q]'s partner to provide him an update as he was not present. The baby, who was being monitored was fine. The foetal heart rate was 130, which was within the normal range of 110 to 160 beats per minute. Variability of the heart was greater than 5 beats per minute and accelerations were present with no sign of decelerations. These are all reassuring factors.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 03.00 hours I documented that [Mother of Baby Q] had two further fresh blood losses and a large blood clot. The total of blood lost was now at 1,595ml. [Mother of Baby Q] was now beginning to tighten/contract. The foetal heart rate was 120, which is good, and the baseline heart rate and variability were
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: all normal. Accelerations in the heart rate were present and there were no signs of any decelerations.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 03.10 I noted that [Mother of Baby Q] had a further blood loss, the total now standing at 1,895ml, and Gelofusine intravenous fluid replacement was started.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 03.20 I noted that [Mother of Baby Q] was starting to feel unwell and a decision was made by Dr Finney to start her on oxygen via a facial mask.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 03.30 hours I noted that [Mother of Baby Q], who was already prepared for surgery, was transferred to theatre for an emergency caesarean section under a general anaesthetic. The foetal heart rate was audible at 140 beats per minute, which again was normal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 03.33 hours I noted that [Mother of Baby Q] was now in theatre and the CTG [that's the monitoring of the baby] was recommenced. The foetal heart rate was 110 beats per minute and the foetus was ++ active, which was all normal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 03.50 hours the foetal heart rate was 110 beats per minute and the baby was coping well.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 04.00 hours I noted that CTG was discontinued for the emergency caesarean section to take place.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 04.09 hours I noted that this was the time of birth, that the baby was male and in good condition for its gestational age.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The baby was taken straight to awaiting paediatricians at the Resuscitaire. As this was an emergency C-section, with that gestation, this is standard practice. The persons present were Dr Huw Mayberry, Dr Andrew [Henton] and neonatal nurse Amy Davies.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 04.11 hours the placenta and membrane were delivered and all appeared complete.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 04.23 I noted that the baby was taken to the neonatal unit by the paediatric team. Throughout this process there were no major concerns for the mother and the baby. And other than the blood loss [Mother of Baby Q] had no other risks. She had no signs of an infection which might include a raised temperature, low blood pressure or perhaps even a high pulse rate."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes her statement, my Lord.

blocks.text: "I took him off CPAP to rest his pressure areas (the CPAP apparatus can cause pressure and discomfort around the nostrils and the bridge of the nose). His work of breathing did not seem
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: to increase following this; he was coping well self-ventilating in air.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "His blood gas analysis [that's measuring the pH/acidity of the blood, carbon dioxide and oxygen levels] showed that he was coping well. This meant I could confidently leave him off CPAP for a longer period. A further capillary blood gas taken later in the shift was also satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I omitted enteral feeds due to obtaining likely bile-stained aspirate from his stomach. This was a precautionary action as bile-stained aspirate can be an indicator of necrotising enterocolitis, seen predominantly in premature infants. blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Just on the neonatal unit at Chester.

blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: There's a handover from 7.30 until 8 between day and night staff; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: And then you assume sole responsibility from 8 o'clock thereafter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Okay. At the start of your shift do you recall any unusual event?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: With [Baby Q]?
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: With anything in the unit. Was your attention drawn to anything during the course of the early part of your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure if it was that day, but before one of my night shifts over the dates around that, yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Okay. So it's an event you've described in your witness statement?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: So tell us what it was that you recalled in your witness statement and then we'll see whether we can assist with the date or timing of it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When I was waiting for handover, I was stood by the nurses' station, which is opposite room 2, the high dependency room, and to the left-hand side of that room there was a baby in an open-top cot, a bit like what we call a Resuscitaire, but it had no top on it and when I looked in, I noticed that the baby didn't look too well. It was an unusual colour and I commented to the nurse next to me that I didn't think he looked too clever, I think were the words I used.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: This is the beginning of a night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Casting your mind back, was it close in time to the occasion when you were the designated nurse for [Baby Q]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was the night shift of the EU referendum.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Okay. We've heard that described by others. I think it was the Wednesday.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The 23rd, I think it was.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: You think it was the 23rd?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: That was the Thursday, so that's the shift we're talking about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was a Thursday.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. I couldn't quite remember which day of the week, I could remember the number but I didn't want to lead any more.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Elections are usually a Thursday.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think it was, yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Okay. So on the 23rd, do you remember roughly what time or what stage in your shift it was? I think you mentioned it was close to handover.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I may have come in at 7 -- I come in a little bit early just to get settled, make a cup of tea ready, get my piece of paper ready for handover.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: So your attention was drawn to this baby who you said wasn't looking very clever?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: What else was going on at the time; can you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: All right. You can't help us with who it was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, they were blonde, that's all I could say.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Do you know which baby it was? Do you know the name of the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't know the name of the baby.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Probably this much (indicating).
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, head.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They were just stood at the bottom of the cot.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Did that fact strike you as unusual or --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: -- troubling?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There was a lot of activity going on in that room, so I just looked at what was going on, commented to the person next to me, and then we started getting ready for handover.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Do you happen to remember who the person was that you commented to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, no.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: When you say there was other activity in the same room, was that other nurses?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It may have been a parent or medical professional, I don't know.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: All right. But it's something that sticks in your mind?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Apart from mentioning it to the person that you were with, did you do anything else about that in particular?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, because there were people -- nurses in there, so...
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Okay. How often at that time were you working at Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was ad hoc, as and when, so I may have done a couple of shifts and then nothing for a couple of weeks and then the odd shift again.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Were you familiar with all the nurses that worked there at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I'd worked there a few weeks previous on the nurse bank as well and I'd done my neonatal degree with a number of the nurses that were on there.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Right. The nurse that you mentioned it to, you don't remember who it was. You don't remember who it was or you don't know who it was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember who it was. It was a female nurse.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: I know the only male nurse wasn't in.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: All right. So if we go back then to [Baby Q]. We've heard that he was born at 04.09 on 22 June, so from the start of your shift at 8 o'clock, say, he'd have been around 39 hours old; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know, but yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: Hopefully my maths is not too far wide of the mark.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I got them in 2019.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, you check all your equipment.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: He had passed, is that, meconium?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. He'd passed meconium.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: "Awaiting paed review."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's from, presumably, one of the medical staff, one of the doctors on duty?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Hopefully, Nurse Downes, you'll recognise your initials in the final column.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes, they are mine.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DOWNES

blocks.text: That's the one you spoke of in your note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY
